description: Mater Amabilis Year 3 living books curriculum for grades 2-3. Introduction to longer novels, biography, and Plutarch's lives. Richer Socratic discussion and written narration begins.

books.title: Little Women
books.author: Louisa May Alcott
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: A rich character study ideal for discussing virtue and the four temperaments. Each sister embodies different strengths and weaknesses. 'Which sister are you most like and why?'

books.title: The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood
books.author: Howard Pyle
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Pyle's prose is deliberately archaic — read aloud slowly. Excellent for discussing justice vs. law. 'Was Robin Hood right to steal from the rich? Why or why not?'

books.title: The Swiss Family Robinson
books.author: Johann David Wyss
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: The family's gratitude to God for provision runs throughout. Excellent natural history woven in — many animals the children encounter can be researched in nature study.

books.title: Plutarch's Lives (selected passages, North translation)
books.author: Plutarch / Thomas North
books.subject: history
books.notes: Mater Amabilis considers Plutarch's Lives essential. Use age-appropriate selected passages. Read slowly, discuss each moral dilemma. 'What made Publicola a good leader?' Written narration begins here.

books.title: Parables from Nature
books.author: Margaret Gatty
books.subject: nature_study
books.notes: Nature stories with rich theological and moral depth — in the Mater Amabilis tradition of nature-faith integration. Ask: 'What does the caterpillar's transformation teach us?'

books.title: Our Island Story
books.author: Henrietta Elizabeth Marshall
books.subject: history
books.notes: Narrative English history from the Romans to Queen Victoria. Marshall writes history as living story. One chapter per session — each is self-contained with a clear hero or crisis.

books.title: Trial and Triumph: Stories from Church History
books.author: Richard Hannula
books.subject: saints
books.notes: Continue or complete this resource. By Year 3 the child may begin written narration of a saint's story. 'Write three sentences telling why this person was brave.'

books.title: The Wind in the Willows
books.author: Kenneth Grahame
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: If not read in Year 2, excellent supplemental here. Grahame's prose lends itself to written narration of the descriptions — 'Describe the River Bank in your own words.'

books.title: Secrets of the Woods
books.author: William J. Long
books.subject: nature_study
books.notes: If not completed in Year 1. Pair with nature notebook entries after each chapter — the child draws and describes the animal observed in the story.

books.title: A Child's History of the World
books.author: V. M. Hillyer
books.subject: history
books.notes: Complete if not finished in earlier years. By Year 3, add timeline entries as each chapter is read — a visual history spine grows with the child.

books.title: Burgess Bird Book for Children
books.author: Thornton W. Burgess
books.subject: nature_study
books.notes: Burgess presents bird facts through story — Peter Rabbit learns about birds from Old Mother Nature. Children absorb real ornithology within a narrative frame.

books.title: The Princess and the Goblin
books.author: George MacDonald
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: MacDonald's tales shaped both Lewis and Tolkien after him — the great-great-grandmother who is trusted before she is understood is classic MacDonald. 'Why does Irene believe her grandmother even when Curdie can't see her?'

books.title: The Stars: A New Way to See Them
books.author: H. A. Rey
books.subject: science
books.notes: Rey's stargazing guide makes constellations memorable through redrawn shapes. Best in Term 3 for evening observation. Connect to the wonder of creation: 'God calls each star by name.'

subject_plans.art_music: Composer: Antonio Vivaldi — vivid, programmatic music that paints a picture (The Four Seasons is an ideal entry point at this age). Artist: Pieter Bruegel the Elder — busy, story-filled scenes of everyday village life, excellent for 'what do you notice first, and what do you notice after looking longer?' Poet: Robert Frost — accessible, image-rich poems that reward a second reading.
subject_plans.greek: Year 3 scope (grade 3) — reading and transliterating. The child now turns a short Greek word into English letters and back (logos to "logos", sophia to "sophia"). That skill is the whole year; everything later depends on it. Sophia, aletheia, and logos join the three virtues, each with its New Testament anchor read aloud (James 1:5; John 14:6; John 1:1). Breathing marks introduced lightly as a noticing — hodos is "hodos", not "odos". Writing Greek letters by hand suits this year well. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Greek New Testament, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a Protestant, Catholic, or Orthodox family can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, icons, a particular church's authority or structure), and take no position on which Greek manuscript tradition is correct: every text supplied reads the same in both. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Greek quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed — and always shown with its transliteration and English.
subject_plans.language_arts: Grade 3: written narration begins in earnest this year (a paragraph, in the child's own hand, following the oral habit built in Years 1-2). Dictation of short studied passages continues. Grammar now names what the child has been noticing — parts of speech, simple sentence structure — through real sentences from that term's living books.
subject_plans.latin: Year 3 scope (grade 3) — words and roots. The spoken habit continues, and root-hunting begins in earnest: veritas gives verify and verdict, fides gives fidelity and confide, caritas gives charity. Sapientia and Veritas join the three virtues this year, each with its Vulgate anchor read aloud (Proverbs 9:10; John 14:6). Short copywork of a Latin phrase by hand suits this year well. Introduce, as a noticing rather than a paradigm, that Latin changes a word's ending to show its job — Deus doing something, Deum being loved — at most one such noticing per session. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Vulgate, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a family of any Christian tradition can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, a particular church's authority or structure); a family that wants that has Saints & Catechism as its own subject. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Latin quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed.
subject_plans.mathematics: Grade 3 scope (Common Core domains 3.OA, 3.NBT, 3.NF, 3.MD, 3.G): multiplication and division fact fluency and the relationship between them; understanding unit fractions and simple fraction comparison; area and perimeter of rectangles; measuring time, liquid volume, and mass; classifying quadrilaterals by their properties. Mater Amabilis approach: keep reasoning aloud — 'why does that work?' — ahead of speed drills.
subject_plans.morning_time: Scripture with brief discussion of its meaning, a hymn or folk song, and a Frost poem. A good place to connect the week's history reading (Our Island Story, Plutarch) to the growing timeline.
subject_plans.scripture: Year 3 scope — people who trusted and people who turned away: Joseph in Egypt from pit to palace; the plagues and the Exodus; the wilderness years; Joshua at Jericho; Gideon; Samson; David the shepherd, singer, and king; Solomon's wisdom; Elijah on Carmel; Daniel and the lions; Jonah. In the Gospels: the parables of the sower, the lost sheep, the prodigal son. Charlotte Mason approach: let the child notice the pattern themselves — ask what this person did when it was hard, rather than naming the virtue for them. Canon and translation are the family's own: follow whatever Bible they are reading and never assert that one tradition's canon, chapter ordering, or translation is the correct one. Teach the narrative and the moral law the text plainly states; leave denomination-specific doctrine — sacramental theology, church governance, a particular catechism's structure — to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister.
